title: 15.1 A 3.9mW 200words/min Neural Signal Processor in Speech Decoding for Brain-Machine Interface
problem: Speech-based brain-machine interfaces require real-time neural network inference on implanted devices with ultra-low power budgets; existing high-end CPUs consume 65 W and require 5.3 seconds to decode a single word, making implantable BMI impractical.
motivation: Speech-based BMIs enable high communication rates (200+ words/min) for paralyzed patients—achieving this requires energy-efficient hardware acceleration of neural network inference to fit within implantable power envelopes.
method: The solution creates a specialized hardware chip that performs speech decoding from brain signals. It works by first running a neural network to infer which individual speech sounds (phones) are present in the brain signal, then using a beam-search decoder (a search method that tracks the most likely word sequences) guided by a language model (which knows which words commonly follow each other in speech) to produce decoded words. This optimized pipeline achieves 200 words per minute.
key_novelty: This is the first specialized hardware processor that accelerates neural-network inference (AI computation) specifically for speech decoding from brain signals, achieving 200 words per minute at 3.9 milliwatts—the power level that makes implantable brain-machine interfaces practical.
contributions: Specialized neural signal processor for phone-probability inference achieving 200 words/min throughput
Efficient language-model beam-search acceleration for word decoding
Ultra-low power design (3.9 mW) enabling implantable BMI operation
Demonstration of 65x power reduction vs. general-purpose CPU for this workload
limitations: Specific neural-network architecture (layer types, precision) and latency per word not detailed in abstract.
primary_theme: Ultra-low-power speech-decoding neural accelerator for implantable BMI
